items.title: ‘I Know God’s Power’: Dallas Jenkins Reacts Moments After Filming Last-Ever ‘The Chosen’ Scene
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The end of an era.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

“The Chosen” creator Dallas Jenkins was filled with gratitude last Thursday night just moments after filming the final scene of his popular biblical series.

Jenkins, who exclusively invited CBN News on set in Texas to witness those last moments, expressed his profound gratitude for how the show is coming to an end.

“I feel awesome because there’s no more days hanging over my head, no more seasons hanging over my head, we’ve done the work that we set out to go,” he said. “God provided everything that we needed.”

The last scene, which featured the disciples on a boat, was memorable because the vessel used in filming was the same seen in the first season of the show. The scene offered a literal and figurative full-circle moment.

“God has met us here in the waters so often,” Jenkins said. “I have nothing but gratitude.”

Ultimately, Jenkins said the mission behind the show has never changed, even as the audience has swelled to over 100 million people.

“We haven’t changed,” he said. “We’re still trying to do the work for God. We’re still humbled, we’re still surrendered, we’re still grinding.”

As for how the seven-season journey changed Jenkins, he said it offered him insight into God’s character and relationship with mankind.

“I’ve been a believer as long as I can remember,” he said. “I know God’s power. … I don’t think I knew quite as much as I do now from doing this show how intimate of a God He is, how personal of a God he is.”

items.title: How Hunting for Deer Helped One Man Overcome His Wife’s Cancer Diagnosis
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Inspiring.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Though many years apart, James Hampton learned similar lessons about God, first through a cancer battle and later when he harvested a 150-inch buck on a hunting trip.

James and his twin brother Chad, now both pastors, grew up in a Christian home and were early followers of Jesus — and quick studies in the deer stand, too. As kids, hunting was a hobby that quickly blossomed into something more, and ultimately became the vehicle for their evangelistic mission today.

“During my wife’s cancer battle, God really spoke to both of us through that battle,” James said during a recent appearance on CBN’s “Faith in Culture” podcast, noting he and his wife were particularly drawn to James 1:2-3, where it’s written, “Dear brothers and sisters, when troubles of any kind come your way, consider it an opportunity for great joy. For you know that when your faith is tested, your endurance has a chance to grow” (NLT).

He continued, “That’s what God does through the waiting, through the trials, through the hard times, and definitely through the cancer battle that my wife went through. He really created perseverance in us, and it’s the same way in hunting.”

At first, that may seem like a peculiar connection — particularly to people who have never hunted.

But, as James said, “there’s a lot of waiting involved in hunting.” The same is true, at times, of waiting for God’s answers to prayer.

The preacher explained he put in more than 100 hours of waiting in the tree stand and, once the timing lined up just right, it was only a matter of seconds — 10, to be exact — before it was all over: he and Chad finally nabbed a 150-inch buck.

“It’s the same way on our hunt for God,” said James. “There’s so much waiting and patience and perseverance.”

As guys with a knack for hunting, they feel naturally at home using sportsman’s language to understand their faith. In fact, their organization, Huntin’ the Truth Ministries, was born out of that correlation.

King David’s writing in Psalm 14:2 has become an anchor for their ministry. In it, he wrote, “The Lord looks down from heaven on the entire human race; he looks to see if anyone is truly wise, if anyone seeks God” (NLT).

The Hampton twins, co-authors of the new devotional, “100 Days of Strength for Hunters,” interpret David’s writing through their passion for hunting. Strong’s Concordance defines “seek” as “investigate,” “enquire,” “study,” “practice,” and “follow.”

“God looks down from heaven on all of us, the sons of men, to see if there are any who understand or any who hunt for Him,” James said.

It was James’ wife’s fight against cancer that God used to bring that Psalm to James’ mind. He said, “[I was] hunting for my own plan for so long.” It wasn’t until he reached the end of himself, he said, that James found himself in the tree stand one night, where he started talking to God about his fears and frustration.

When he’s out hunting, James said, he always carries a small camo Bible in his backpack. He opened the Scriptures and God guided him to Psalm 14.

“It was that night God kind of slapped me across the face and made me realize … that He wanted me to hunt for Him like I hunt for deer,” James recalled. “He wants us all to hunt for Him, to search for Him, to seek for Him. … And I knew what He was talking about, because I knew how much of a diehard hunter I was and how much passion I had for hunting and how many hours I put in for hunting.”

He added, “God was telling me, ‘I want you to do the same thing: I want you to hunt for Me that hard. Seek Me that hard, with all your heart.'”

Listen to our full conversation in the “Faith in Culture” podcast episode above.

items.title: If Jesus Didn’t Do It Alone, Maybe We Shouldn’t Either, Says Toni Collier
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: When a mentor told Toni Collier to start praying for friends, she thought it sounded like something a kid would pray. “What a weak, weird prayer,” she remembers thinking. “What am I, a child?” When Collier started following Jesus in earnest, she wanted to quit cursing, drinking and doing drugs. She
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

When a mentor told Toni Collier to start praying for friends, she thought it sounded like something a kid would pray. “What a weak, weird prayer,” she remembers thinking. “What am I, a child?”

When Collier started following Jesus in earnest, she wanted to quit cursing, drinking and doing drugs. She said spending time with her old friends kept drawing her back into habits she wanted to leave. “I ended up alone,” she told RELEVANT.

Asking for friends went against the way Collier had learned to move through life. She said she left her parents’ house at 16, finished college at 19 and later earned a master’s degree. She was used to moving quickly and taking care of herself. “I’m fast. I’m capable. I got it. That’s what I thought of myself. I can handle it.”

After she started praying, Collier found herself working up the nerve to introduce herself to a stranger. At a church conference, she noticed a woman in the green room with platinum blonde hair and tattoos up her arm. Collier thought they looked like complete opposites, but she felt drawn to talk to her.

“I just felt like I needed to go talk to her,” she said. “It was awkward. So awkward.”

They’ve been friends for nine years. When Collier went through a public divorce she described as humiliating, that woman was the first person she called. Her friend had been through a divorce too, and understood what it was like to keep going in ministry afterward. The relationship Collier once felt silly asking God for had become one she depended on.

The Strong Friend

Collier knows how much pride can get tangled up in being the person who can handle everything. In the interview, she described the shame that kept her from admitting she needed people, even as she wanted them close. Asking could mean finding out that someone didn’t want to stay.

“I don’t want to be needy because then I’ll be discounted,” she said. “I don’t want to need people because maybe they won’t come back because they’ll get tired of me.”

She had carried that fear into her understanding of strength. Then her own life became more than she could manage by herself. “And now we look stupid because we don’t have anybody around us to catch us when we are no longer the strong friend,” she said.

It’s an expectation she has trouble reconciling with Jesus’ life. The Gospels describe him gathering disciples and living alongside friends. For Collier, that example gives Christians room to need each other without treating dependence as a failure of faith.

“Jesus did not need the 12 disciples to fulfill the purpose that was on the inside of him,” she said. “And yet he still did it with people, probably to teach us all that if Jesus didn’t do it alone, maybe we shouldn’t either.”

In her own friendships, accepting help has sometimes meant letting someone introduce her to something she hadn’t known to ask for. Collier said counseling wasn’t familiar to her growing up. A friend named Erin asked who her counselor was, treating the question as casually as asking about a trainer at the gym. Their conversation helped her see professional support as something she could seek.

She also turns to friends with more years behind them. Now in her mid-30s, she described calling friends in their 50s and 60s when she faced something unfamiliar. They had lived through situations she was encountering for the first time. Those relationships gave her people she could ask, “What would you do in this situation?”

Someone Who Can Stay

Letting friends into a painful part of your life comes with a question of its own: what will they do once they know? Collier is wary of the impulse to immediately offer an answer. She recognizes it in herself, especially when she wants to help someone through a hard season.

“I love a good redemption story and I want to be a part,” she said. “We’re not God and we are no one’s savior.”

At the time of the interview, she had been reading Job. What held her attention was the beginning of his friends’ visit: they heard about his suffering, traveled to him and sat on the ground with him for seven days and nights without speaking. She had expected them to arrive with resources to rebuild his life. Their first response was to sit with him.

“When someone’s in pain, when someone’s suffering, they really just need witness,” she said. “They need their friends to be there.”

She uses that word in her book, Don’t Try This Alone, borrowing from her group therapy circle’s description of witness as “the art of being with someone in their pain.” In John 11, she sees it in Jesus weeping with those mourning Lazarus before raising him from the dead. “I think Jesus was trying to show us something much more important than him answering all of our prayers, that he’s with us,” she said.

For a friend listening to someone describe a lost job or difficulty having a baby, that can mean resisting the rush to recommend a devotional or offer a doctor’s number. Collier suggests starting with “I’m really sorry,” and acknowledging how much it hurts. There will be problems a friend can’t solve. The friendship still gives them a way to be present.

Collier doesn’t make opening up sound painless. “Vulnerability really sucks sometimes,” she said. She compared it to uncovering wounds she had spent years trying to hide. Being willing to do that requires friends she trusts to keep her confidence and stay involved after the conversation gets difficult.

“We’re not looking for safe spaces. We’re looking for safe people,” she said. “People that won’t go tell your business. People that can show up for you.”

Finding them takes some ordinary, uncomfortable effort. Collier recommends places where people gather regularly, including church, and making yourself available for a conversation. Her own prayer for friends led her into a room where she still had to walk over and say hello.

“I had to start conversations or be open to conversations that were being had with me,” she said. “That’s on me. That’s on us. We got to start getting brave enough to say, ‘What’s your name? You live around here? You have kids?’”

Years later, when her marriage ended, she had someone she could call who already knew her. She didn’t have to explain what continuing in ministry after a divorce might feel like. Her friend had been there.

items.title: The Politics of Envy and Contentment
items.author: Henry T. Edmondson III
items.summary:
Henry T. Edmondson III

Given the precarious times in which we live, it is important to understand envy and embrace its opposite: contentment.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Henry T. Edmondson III

The phrase “the politics of envy” appears from time to time in political conversation, and we are likely to hear it more in days to come, given the success a few candidates for the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) have enjoyed in recent primary elections. Socialism and its parent political philosophy, Marxism, condemn a world of “inequality.” At some point, this may stir up sentiments of envy on the part of the “have-nots,” as they see that they fall short of the “haves.” To be sure, Winston Churchill famously called socialism the “gospel of envy.” Some who run on a socialist platform rely on stirring up these sentiments. For that reason, and given the precarious times in which we live, it is important to understand envy and embrace its opposite: contentment.

Envy is a grave challenge to an individual’s well-being and to the health of a society. The most important work written on the subject is Envy: A Theory of Social Behaviour by German–American sociologist and anthropologist, Helmut Schoeck. His is a comprehensive study of envy: He argues that envy is an inescapable part of the human condition and that it is not understood as well as it should be. He warns the reader of the destructive tendencies of envy and notes that part of Marxist doctrine is to encourage envy—if not, social change can’t occur. For that reason, it is immoral to tell people they should not be envious; that is to say, it is morally wrong to encourage people to be content with what they have. Stated yet again, the success of socialism depends on cultivating a “virtue of envy.”

Matt Oberdick, director of the Center for Culture and the Family, warns,

Socialist rhetoric is becoming increasingly mainstream. And a growing number of young Americans are embracing ideas that previous generations would have recognized as fundamentally incompatible with liberty . . . These are not ideas developing in a distant or abstract place. They are taking root here in the United States—in our cities, our universities, and our public debates. 

Indeed, the universities are one of the few places on the planet where Marxist/Socialist ideas are kept on life support. 

The Social and Political Dimensions of Envy

Envy doesn’t stand alone; it seeks an object. For that reason, the seventh commandment doesn’t simply say, “Don’t be envious.” Rather, it reads, “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, or male or female slave, or ox, or donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor” (Exod 20:17). We are envious when someone else has something that we find enticing. A late model SUV may attract my attention in the showroom. I may get dreamy, I may become wistful, but if the same car shows up in my neighbor’s driveway, the misery begins. Time to look at the budget and figure out the Kelley Blue Book trade-in value on my own SUV.  

Socialists argue that any significant inequality is wrong. One solution is to reduce inequality by improving the conditions of the have-nots, but it may work just as well to lessen the circumstances of the haves. Either may be satisfactory, but the latter may even be best. It is a matter of “justice.” Even more, some condemn any economic system as evil that allows individuals to accumulate substantial wealth, as is the case in the US.

Although there have been well-intended people who thought socialism might be good for the downtrodden, much of the rhetoric today seems to be little more than a condemnation of those who have wealth. No one, however, seems to be saying much about the plight of the genuinely poor or how they might best be helped. Despite the vast amounts of money the country has spent trying to alleviate poverty, the best way to help the misfortunate is still too often a mystery. Do today’s socialists really care? It is hard to know.

In Democracy in America, Alexis de Tocqueville observed that, ironically, the more equal a society becomes, the more its citizens notice the disparity between the haves and the have-nots—or perhaps better said: the “have-more” and “have-less.” In other words, reducing inequality doesn’t seem to eliminate envy.

As it festers, envy takes delight in the misfortune of those who enjoy advantages not available to others. The German philosopher Immanuel Kant explains that envy is a tendency “to view the well-being of others with distress, even though it does not detract from one’s own.” Kant says that the envious person uses the wrong standard to evaluate their own situation. Although I should ask if I am satisfied with my own well-being, I ask instead how my situation compares with another’s. This is an invidious comparison, though, because there will always be someone better situated than me. I will never be satisfied. 

Envy, Kant continues, is only satisfied when another’s good fortune is destroyed. Schoeck succinctly explains, “The envious man thinks that if his neighbor breaks a leg, he will be able to walk better himself.”

One further step: If I want to persuade you that we need radical political change in favor of something more “just,” I need to convince you that you are miserable—even if you are not. It doesn’t matter how good you think your circumstances may be, don’t you realize how unhappy you are? It’s not hard to see how envy overwhelms gratitude.

It Is Worse Than You Think

Envy is immoral; it is a sin, it is a vice, and it is a fast track to an ungrateful, dismal life. It is not a virtue—and the more you know, the worse it gets. Not only is it condemned in the tenth commandment, it is also one of the seven deadly sins.

New Testament admonitions are harsh; Jesus warns his listeners to guard their hearts: “Take heed, and beware of all covetousness; for a man’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15). Jesus further explains that the sins that defile a person come from the untamed desires in the heart. 

James warns, 

You desire and do not have; so you kill. And you covet and cannot obtain; so you fight and wage war. You do not have, because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions. Unfaithful creatures! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God (Jas 4:2–4).

Both the Epistle to the Ephesians and the Epistle to the Colossians regard the sin of covetousness as a kind of idolatry and associate it with sexual immorality and impurity which provokes the “wrath of God.” 

The first line of defense against envy, then, starts in the heart. The book of Proverbs explains, “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.” 

The political upshot of all of this is that anyone who promotes political change by inciting envy and those who allow themselves to be allured by envy are in very dangerous territory because they are blinded, and they become incapable of gratitude. Anne Hendershott writes, 

Envy derives from the Latin invidia, which means “non sight.” This etymology suggests that envy arises from, and creates, a form of blindness or lack of perspective. In Purgatorio, Dante Alighieri had the envious punished by having to wear penitential gray cloaks, their eyes sewn shut with iron wire because the truly envious are blind to the goodness, truth, and beauty around them—warning that the envious are blind to reason and love, spending their days tormented by resentment toward those who possess that which they covet.

Order Your Set Today

Contentment Is “Great Gain”

Some suggest that as religion recedes in American society, people are putting their faith in socialism. Nothing else really explains why some Americans are finding socialism attractive. But this, as the country song goes, “is looking for love in all the wrong places.” Proponents of socialism in the US point to Denmark, Sweden, and Norway as examples of socialist countries we should emulate, but they don’t understand the nature of those countries. As the Danish prime minister has insisted, “We are a market economy.” The possibilities go down very quickly from there. The late Hugo Chavez tried to make Venezuela socialist and ruined the country. Other possibilities are Cuba and North Korea. Who wants to live there? Only in the US are people getting excited about socialism, but it is an enthusiasm rooted in ignorance.

1 Timothy provides a classic warning against the love of money and stresses that “if we have food and clothing, with these we shall be content.” But, on balance, the scriptural attention to envy is quite grim, and that suggests just how dangerous covetousness can be. 

As is often the case, St. Thomas Aquinas provides practical guidance by softening the biblical blow, so to speak, and offering a forward-looking approach to the issue. The Angelic Doctor explains how the virtue of contentment is an antidote to envy. Contentment, as a virtue, is an expression of the cardinal virtue of temperance. It is a habit that moderates our interest in the things around us, helping us to maintain a middle place between, in this case, unhinged asceticism on one side and envy and greed on the other. This is what Aristotle calls a “golden mean.”

Like all the other virtues, most people lean in one direction more than the other, so in this case, the typical tendency is toward the latter, the excess of covetousness. This calls for us to moderate our desire for external goods, not demand excessive or superfluous requirements for happiness. While true happiness will only be found in the beatific contemplation of God himself, an “imperfect” happiness is possible in this life, or as the Baltimore Catechism says, we can be “reasonably happy.”

Human beings possess a desire for truth and goodness that temporary pleasures cannot satisfy. These restless yearnings find their peace and fulfillment only in God. This is because, as St. Augustine said, “Our hearts are restless until they find their rest in you.” C. S. Lewis, in Mere Christianity, writes, “If we find ourselves with a desire that nothing in this world can satisfy, the most probable explanation is that we were made for another world.”

items.title: Friday, October 2, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, today we celebrate the Memorial of the Holy Guardian Angels.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Job 38:1, 12-21; 40:3-5

Then the Lord answered Job out of the whirlwind:
“Have you commanded the morning since your days began,
    and caused the dawn to know its place,
so that it might take hold of the skirts of the earth,
    and the wicked be shaken out of it?
It is changed like clay under the seal,
    and it is dyed like a garment.
Light is withheld from the wicked,
    and their uplifted arm is broken.
“Have you entered into the springs of the sea,
    or walked in the recesses of the deep?
Have the gates of death been revealed to you,
    or have you seen the gates of deep darkness?
Have you comprehended the expanse of the earth?
    Declare, if you know all this.
“Where is the way to the dwelling of light,
    and where is the place of darkness,
that you may take it to its territory
    and that you may discern the paths to its home?
Surely you know, for you were born then,
    and the number of your days is great!
Then Job answered the Lord:
“See, I am of small account; what shall I answer you?
    I lay my hand on my mouth.
I have spoken once, and I will not answer;
    twice, but will proceed no further.”

Psalm
Psalm 139:1-3, 7-8, 9-10, 13-14ab

O Lord, you have searched me and known me.
You know when I sit down and when I rise up;
    you discern my thoughts from far away.
You search out my path and my lying down,
    and are acquainted with all my ways.
Where can I go from your spirit?
    Or where can I flee from your presence?
If I ascend to heaven, you are there;
    if I make my bed in Sheol, you are there.
If I take the wings of the morning
    and settle at the farthest limits of the sea,
even there your hand shall lead me,
    and your right hand shall hold me fast.
For it was you who formed my inward parts;
    you knit me together in my mother’s womb.
I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.
    Wonderful are your works;
that I know very well.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 18:1-5, 10

At that time the disciples came to Jesus and asked, “Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” He called a child, whom he put among them, and said, “Truly I tell you, unless you change and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever becomes humble like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven. Whoever welcomes one such child in my name welcomes me.

“Take care that you do not despise one of these little ones; for, I tell you, in heaven their angels continually see the face of my Father in heaven.

Reflection

Friends, today we celebrate the Memorial of the Holy Guardian Angels.

Well, is it reasonable to believe in angels? Look at the wild variety in the visible universe—the millions of species of animals, the billions of galaxies, the myriad shells that wash up on the seashore, the incalculable number of cells in each human body. Is it likely that, between this staggeringly variegated physical dimension of creation and God, there simply yawns a great ontological abyss? Isn’t it likely to hold that God has manifested at least an equally great creativity in regard to the purely spiritual order? 

But why would God send these spiritual messengers to help us? Why wouldn’t he just take care of us himself? Those questions, of course, are born of a frame of mind that sets God and his world in competition.

On the Catholic reading, God delights in using secondary causes, so that his creatures can participate in his active providence of the universe. Aquinas says that each of us, due to our changeable and fallible nature, has been assigned a heavenly guide. Once we’re in heaven, we won’t require a guide anymore, and our angel will become our friend.
